passages.t: ‘The LORD is my shepherd’, and the darkest valley
passages.happening:
The heading reads simply, “A Psalm of David” (verse 1). Then: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (verse 1).

The shepherd does everything for the sheep. “He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters” (verse 2). “He restores my soul; He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name” (verse 3).

Then the path goes down into the dark. “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me” (verse 4).

Notice the change in that verse. Up to now the psalm has spoken about God: ‘He makes’, ‘He leads’. In the dark valley it starts speaking to him: ‘You are with me.’
passages.hearers:
This is a psalm of trust. It is often read at funerals, and it is often made soft and pretty. The first hearers would not have heard it that way.

Shepherding in Judah was hard and dangerous work in dry, rocky land. Green grass and calm water were not just there. The shepherd had to know where to find them and lead the flock to them, sometimes a long way. David knew this work. He told Saul that when a lion or a bear took a lamb, “I went after it, struck it down, and delivered the lamb from its mouth” (1 Samuel 17:35).

‘Shepherd’ was also a word for a king. Kings across the ancient world called themselves shepherds of their people. The Babylonian king Hammurabi does so in his law code. God told David, “You will shepherd My people Israel” (2 Samuel 5:2). So Psalm 23 turns the picture round. The king is a sheep. The LORD is his shepherd.

‘The valley of the shadow of death’ translates one Hebrew word, tsalmavet. It may be built from ‘shadow’ and ‘death’, or it may simply mean ‘deep darkness’. Many modern Bibles put ‘the darkest valley’ or ‘deep darkness’. Picture a narrow gorge in the hills where the sun does not reach and wild animals hide. It is any place of great danger, death included.

The rod was a club for beating off wild animals. The staff was a long stick for guiding the sheep and pulling them out of trouble. Both comfort the sheep, because both mean the shepherd is there.
passages.later:
The prophet Ezekiel speaks against Israel's selfish leaders, the bad shepherds, and gives God's promise: “I will tend My flock and make them lie down, declares the Lord GOD” (Ezekiel 34:15). Isaiah says, “He tends His flock like a shepherd; He gathers the lambs in His arms” (Isaiah 40:11).

Jesus took the picture for himself, and added something no ordinary shepherd does: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep” (John 10:11). He told of a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to look for the one that is lost (Luke 15:4).

Hebrews calls Jesus “that great Shepherd of the sheep” whom God “brought back from the dead” (Hebrews 13:20). Revelation ends the picture: “the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd” (Revelation 7:17).
passages.hard:
‘I shall not want.’ Does that mean a believer will never lack anything, never be poor or sick or sad?

No. The same psalm walks through the darkest valley. The promise is not that the sheep will never be in danger. It is that the shepherd will never leave. ‘I shall not want’ means: I will not lack what I truly need, and above all I will not lack him.

The psalm is also not a promise that a loved one will be healed. Many who prayed it have died. The comfort of verse 4 is not ‘you will not go into the valley’. It is ‘You are with me’ in it.

If you are grieving, this psalm does not ask you to feel calm. Read it slowly, and let the shepherd be with you in the valley you are in. Grief is not a failure of faith. If your grief has become too heavy to carry, please tell someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
Read the psalm as a sheep, not as a poet. Sheep are not strong or clever. They survive because someone looks after them. The psalm asks you to admit that you need looking after.

Then ask where you are in it today: in the green pasture, on the right path, or in the valley. The psalm is true in all three places.

passages.t: ‘You prepare a table before me’, and ‘goodness and mercy will follow me’
passages.happening:
The picture changes from a pasture to a meal. “You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows” (verse 5).

The psalm ends looking forward over a whole life. “Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Now God is a host and the psalmist is his guest. The table is set while enemies look on. They can see, but they cannot touch him. Being welcomed and fed in front of them is a public sign of whose side God is on.

Pouring oil on a guest's head was a mark of welcome and honour. Jesus once reminded a host that he had not done it for him: “You did not anoint My head with oil” (Luke 7:46). A cup filled to overflowing is a host's generous welcome.

‘Mercy’ in verse 6 is hesed, God's faithful, covenant love. ‘Follow’ is stronger in Hebrew. It means to pursue, to chase. Enemies once chased David. Now God's goodness and love chase him down, every day.

‘The house of the LORD’ was God's dwelling with his people: the tent of meeting, and later the temple in Jerusalem.
passages.later:
Jesus spoke of his Father's house: “In My Father's house are many rooms” (John 14:2). He said he was going there “to prepare a place for you” (John 14:2).

The last pages of the Bible picture God's people at a great feast (Revelation 19:9). And they promise what the psalm hopes for: God “will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 7:17).
passages.asks:
Verse 6 asks you to look back as well as forward. Where has goodness ‘followed’ you without your noticing?

The psalm also shows that peace with God does not mean having no enemies. The table is set in their presence. You can be at peace while trouble is still in the room.

Many people learn this psalm by heart. If you have not, try it. It is six verses long, and it will be there when you need it most.
